newsitem.title: UK: EMU 1999 launch chances high but receding - survey. [CORRECTED 12:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: EMU 1999 launch chances high but receding - survey. [CORRECTED 12:00 GMT]

text.p: Analysts believe the chances of European monetary union going ahead on time remain high but their optimism has dimmed slightly in the past month as doubts about Germany's ability to meet the qualifying targets grow, a Reuters survey showed on Thursday (corrects to make clear the survey represents analysts' views).

In the survey, carried out between March 10 and 11, the mean of 45 forecasts showed that the average likelihood of economic and monetary union (EMU) going ahead on its scheduled launch date of January 1, 1999 had fallen to 76 percent, from 83 percent in February and January and 86 percent in December.

"Germany may not meet the convergence criteria and there is the possibility of a challenge in the constitutional court. To meet the budget deficit criteria, fiscal policy needs to be tighter," said Stephen King, chief European economist at HSBC James Capel.
"Tighter policy will have a negative impact on economic growth and unemployment. This translates into handing over votes to the SPD (opposition Social Democrats)."

All 45 contributors in the survey of analysts across Europe agreed Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg and Netherlands would be in the first wave of EMU and all but one also believed Austria would be included.
A majority of 38 and 37 analysts respectively expected Ireland and Finland to be included.
Germany's chances of attaining the entry targets for EMU have been hit by dismal jobless figures. German unemployment is at levels not seen since the depression of the 1930s.
In February it was an unadjusted 4.672 million against 4.658 million in January. The unadjusted jobless rate remained unchanged at 12.2 percent.

"With an election due next year (Chancellor) Helmut Kohl will have to think carefully whether he wants to alienate the electorate and destroy his re-election chances with more austerity measures," a Frankfurt-based economist said.

The median of forecasts collected in a Reuters survey of convergence criteria carried out in February showed Germany's budget deficit at 3.05 percent of gross domestic product(GDP) in 1997 and total debt at 62 percent of GDP.

These overreach the Maastricht treaty EMU targets of three percent and 60 percent respectively for 1997. The European Commission will assess countries for their eligibility in early 1998 before the German election due later that same year.
Flexibility in interpreting the criteria is allowed for in the treaty, but at issue is the definition of flexible, analysts say.
In February, Wilhelm Noelling, a former Bundesbank council member, threatened to take the government to the constitutional court if Germany went ahead on EMU without meeting the targets.
Other council members have also strongly expressed the view that the criteria should be interpreted strictly.

Forty one of the contributors saw a greater than evens chance of EMU going ahead on time. Of these, 19 considered it very likely that the criteria would be loosely interpreted, eight considered it likely and 12 considered it quite likely.
Only one said it was not likely the criteria would be loosely interpreted.
Four contributors put the chances of a delay at more than 50 percent. Two said EMU would be delayed until 2001, one said it would only be delayed for a year and one said it would never happen.
"If there is a delay, it will take a few more years to sort out economies and convergence and build up enough trust within Europe for EMU to go ahead and be workable," said HSBC's King.
Public opinion polls are showing that "trust" in the euro, the single currency, is a major hurdle in Germany.
The people are not prepared to give up their strong mark for a currency which will be weakened by the possible inclusion of weaker currencies such as the Italian lira, analysts said.
The question of Italian convergence is also a central question in the EMU debate.

"We are not sure whether Italian convergence is real or sustainable and this has long term implications for the stability of monetary union," said Felix Gonzalez, chief economist at Beta Capital in Spain.
Some also said they had revised down their expectations because they did not see Italy allowing themselves to be excluded from the first wave.
"A delay may be the best alternative because EMU cannot go ahead without Germany. If Germany qualifies on the basis of a loose interpretation, then why not Italy," said the Frankfurt based analyst.
